speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate, because I believe it is the fourth time I have had occasion to speak to a motion by the Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for the production of papers according to certain laws, must remain confidential. Today, production of papers is being requested in connection with the Foreign Investment Review Act, and here again, I think we must be extremely circumspect as to the approach used in dealing with such cases. The fact remains that when a corporate citizen asks a government to examine its case, the company is not particularly anxious to have its file become the subject of public debate, and for a very simple reason. At the risk of
December 16, 1982

repeating myself for the fourth time for the benefit of the Member for Vaudreuil, I would say that there are two basic aspects to this kind of discussion. First of all, there is the matter of completion between private companies. There is not a single company that is anxious to publicize its industrial, development or investment strategies. Therefore, a government cannot publish information provided by a company on the understanding that its confidentiality will be preserved. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to point out to the Member for Vaudreuil that Parliament itself passed the Foreign Investment Review Act, and that if the Government were to table such documents, it would be failing to comply with legislation passed by this Parliament. It would therefore be a glaring contradiction within our parliamentary institutions, and 1 think there is not a single industry or company or citizen who would still trust Parliament if it were to ignore the legal principle of absolute confidentiality, which is the very basis of this institution, and I think this is something that should not be taken lightly. If the element of trust were lost when papers are tabled here in the House, I have the impression that there would no longer be many people or countries that would be anxious to deal with the Parliament of Canada. A second aspect, equally fundamental, is that of competition, as I pointed out earlier.
There are various programs sponsored by Federal departments where a detailed study takes place before a decision is made. The FIRA program is one, and there are others administered by DREE, by the Department of the Secretary of State, and by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. Until a decision is made, documents may not be made public. There are two more reasons for this. First of all, as I said earlier, the Act prescribes that all documents shall be kept confidential. Second, and this is perhaps the most important part, the company or corporate citizens submitting an application demand that the confidentiality of their files will be preserved. Similarly, personal income tax returns are treated confidentially by the Department of National Revenue.
The same method is applied to industries, that is, the method applied in the case of a private corporation or, as I said earlier, in the case of a private citizen. It is not a case of preferential treatment, since both private citizens and corporations are treated exactly the same. 1 would like to repeat something that has already been said here in the House by the Minister of International Trade under the Government of the Right Hon. Joe Clark, and I am referring to Mr. Michael Wilson who was the Minister at the time. He clearly indicated that the confidentiality of documents had to be preserved. I would like to quote the Hon. Member to be sure of his exact words, because I think it is important to recall what was said at that time. On November 22, 1979, to be exact, the Minister of State said that he was surprised, and 1 quote:
Foreign Investment Review Agency
-that the Hon. Member would ask that the Government ignore the specific requirements of an act passed by this Parliament.
He went on to comment, and I quote:
That provision was purposely incorporated in the Foreign Investment Review Act to safeguard the commercial interests of investors who are obliged to submit their investment proposals for review under the act.
When an investor files notice of his intentions, and in any discussions that may occur later, he usually, if not invariably, imparts to the government through the agency a good deal of highly confidential information regarding his plans and intentions relating to the investment he is proposing. Therefore, he has the right to expect that information of that sort will not become known, prematurely at least, to others, notably potential competitors.
I could quote several other passages. I think these quotes are necessary because, as 1 said earlier, this is the fifth time we are dealing with a formal request for production of papers here in the House. I think that if the Minister were to give way to such pressure or such requests, departments would be unable to properly analyze files while safeguarding the very real interests of a company, the very heart of a company, that is, its balance sheets, investment plans, markets and technology. I think that is elementary, and I hope the Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) is listening so that we will not have to deal with such motions again. After all, we would all like to make the time of the House more productive, instead of repeating the same thing over and over again. Of course, I could have read the first four speeches I made on the subject, but I decided against it, out of respect for the House and also because it is useful to discuss other aspects that are perhaps more important to Canadians, instead of always dealing with the same topics arising from motions or requests that, for all practical purposes, always amount to the same thing.
On the other hand, 1 would like to go back, if the House will allow me, to what was said earlier by the Member for Rimous-ki-Temiscouata (Mrs. Cote). I know that a great deal was said about FIRA and the Foreign Investment Review Act. Some say it is too hermetic and too confidential, and that the regulations are not sufficiently known. However, only yesterday, someone came to see me at my office in my capacity of Parliamentary Secretary, to tell me that the Act was still too permissive. Clearly, there is more than one way of looking at the matter. I believe the problem is a medium-term one. What I would suggest, along the lines of what was said earlier by the Member for Rimouski-Temiscouata, is to submit certain proposals to parliamentary commissions on industry, trade and commerce. These would concern aspects that should be improved and would be submitted by the people interested in improving them and in establishing the appropriate mechanisms.
That is a very good idea, which would enable us to review past achievements and in the light of our experience of the past few years, to make a truly objective assessment and to take the necessary corrective action. It is a fact that in any organization such as FIRA, there is room for improvement, but I am

December 16, 1982
Foreign Investment Review Agency
practically sure that Hon. Members have interesting suggestions to make in this connection and that a parliamentary committee sitting at the time when the estimates are considered and the votes discussed would probably provide an ideal forum to carry out this study and take into account the suggestions made by the Hon. Member for Rimouski-Temis-couata (Mrs. Cote). I know that F1RA has been criticized from all quarters for some time. 1 think we should go beyond criticism and try to improve existing mechanisms in order to better meet the need of Hon. Members. I know that it is very difficult to trust an organization blindly, whether it be a government, a department, a corporation, for there are cases such as the Iron Ore and the mining companies which the Hon. Member of the New Democratic Party who spoke before me mentioned and to which I will return later. But it remains nevertheless that a file should be kept confidential, otherwise it would never be possible to deal seriously and responsibly with the moral or physical entity that submitted it.
I have just referred to the previous speaker from the New Democratic Party who referred to mining companies. I too wish some corporations would disclose part of their figures, and I even asked the House permission once to examine their five-year projections, in order to ascertain their intentions over a longer period of time, because it must be realized that in communities such as those in Gaspe or on the North Shore problems are created each time a corporation operates in complete secrecy, changing its structure as it sees fit, because everybody is taken by surprise. I feel that some checking is required to remedy such situations. It is incredible how those people feel insecure because no planning was provided for some developments. In as much as certain papers are asked to be tabled in the House, I would like personally to see the scope of the debate extended for the benefit of some companies which will remain unnamed because I think everyone acted in good faith but I think that the legislator should be well informed in order to make responsible decisions. There are companies which would derive some advantage in publishing their investment plans although not in every detail because what is valid for the government is also valid for companies. However, I do not think it would be wise for companies to make public the whole of their financial operations or of their investment projections, but the government needs a minimum of information to act responsibly on behalf of our citizens. And a recession such as the current one leads us to reflect on those matters.
Moreover I would like, Mr. Speaker, to suggest that in another debate on Private Members' Business, we could deal with the whole issue of confidential public papers not only when the Foreign Investment Review Agency is concerned but also in the case of the private sector and some other government levels. I am referring to the federal and provincial governments because especially in the Far North, Northern Quebec or Northern Ontario, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources is extremely interested in their development and I think that the Department would find it advisable to meet more often with private businesses and state quite
clearly what sort of development is to be expected in those areas.
I am very much amazed at all the work which is being done in certain economic departments here in Ottawa, and in the ten provinces, and invididual private corporations, but the time might be ripe in my view for some kind of pooling, which would allow for better planning and much more responsibility to those regions and everyone across the board. This could be the subject of an interesting debate in this House, because this would enable us to describe the work everyone is doing in his own area but which should be considered in the overall context. Certainly madam Speaker would be quite happy to have a very animated debate on the subject. Certainly we would enjoy the Chair's full cooperation to discuss all that.
To come back to the motion of the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), I would appreciate his stating in writing what he would like to know from this particular company, because the phrasing of his motion is rather general. It reads, and I quote:
That an humble Address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of all agreements, correspondence, notes and other communications relating to the requirement by the Foreign Investment Review Agency that Tate and Lyall Limited reduce its share holdings in Redpath Sugar Limited.
Clearly this is a request of a general nature, but I would like written specifics that would be useful to the Hon. Member. Because such a general request amounts to asking for all the documents, and this is why the Agency has turned down his request for the sake of confidentiality as I explained earlier, or of mere competition. But if the Hon. Member requires specific answers or documents to carry out his work in a more enlightened and relevant way, the department and the Agency would be pleased to make them available to him. I would just like to mention for the benefit of all Hon. Members that, as concerns DREE, for instance, a lot of material must be submitted when a company applies for a grant including public interest information and there is no objection to that. However, and 1 want to emphasize that often the companies are requesting that no part of these papers be made public. In this case, the company might be willing to cooperate with the Member and provide some information, and this was done in the past by various Departments. However, the Hon. Member has made a general request for the tabling of all the records and it is to this that the Department and the company object.
1 would like to point out to the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil, who is listening very carefully, that it is the company which requests confidentiality. The Department looked into that because when such an answer has to be given to a Member who obviously is very interested in his motion, the Government takes the trouble to check with the company involved to make sure the answer given by the Department meets the intentions
December 16, 1982

of the company. In this case, I did what I had already done four times before concerning other motions of this type moved by the same Member and requesting the tabling of documents which are considered privileged by the Department and the company.
Mr. Speaker, since I have very little time left, I would like to take a few minutes to tell the House about the intentions of the Foreign Investment Review Agency for the next few years because recently people have been asking the Department whether the Agency really does allow foreign investment in Canada, in view of some suggstion to the contrary. Many people say that if such were the case, the Agency does nothing to promote the use of foreign capital for the development of our country.
I just want to tell the House that after looking into the matter we have found that most of the foreign companies which agree to abide by the social requirements of Canada and to reinvest in this country are then authorized to locate just about anywhere in the country. The Agency is particularly careful not to let a foreign company settling in Canada undermine existing industries. The Agency is very cautious in this regard. I believe that my time has expired, Madam Speaker.

That includes something like 200,000 people across this country.
These people are responsible for providing Canadians with a wide variety of fresh fruit and vegetables year round. It is a big job when you consider that most of the produce they handle is highly perishable. Last year they imported and distributed $1.1 billion worth of fruits and nuts, and some $600 million worth of vegetables.
Their job has been made easier in recent years by advances in refrigeration and cold-storage methods, and by improvement in the transportation system. Unfortunately, the legislation that regulates the industry has not advanced as quickly as the industry itself has.
The fruit and vegetable industry is in need of tighter regulations-regulations that will help ensure that costly delays and interruptions do not occur in the delivery of fresh produce, from the producer to the consumer.
That is why we have before us for third reading, Bill C-98, a Bill to amend the Canadian Agricultural Products Standard Act, commonly known as the CAPS Act.
This Bill has received first and second reading in the past month and passed through the committee stage last week, where the Canadian Fruit Wholesalers Association and the Canadian Horticultural Council spoke in support of the Bill. The speed with which this Bill was passed, Mr. Speaker, is to be noted. It won all Party agreement in just three meetings of the Standing Committee on Agriculture, which speaks for the soundness and the importance of the proposed amendments.
Bill C-98 is an important Bill for the industry. It is important because it would give the CAPS Act the legal power necessary to regulate the terms and conditions under which the fruit and vegetable trade in Canada can operate efficiently for the benefit of producers and consumers.
One of the most significant amendments concerns a board of arbitration to resolve disputes between buyers and sellers of fresh produce. When one Party is unhappy with the arrival condition of a shipment, if they feel that the shipment is not in as good a condition as it should be, and when the buyer rejects the delivered goods the arbitration procedure is recognized by the industry as an effective means of handling such disputes.
The board of arbitration has continued to operate on a voluntary basis in settling disputes since the previous legislation was declared invalid in 1974. But without legal powers, the board has not been able to do its job effectively. There have, for instance, been cases of parties ignoring decisions which the board could not enforce.
You must realize that when you are dealing with highly perishable products that must travel long distances, it is necessary that an arbitration board be able to act quickly and with authority. Otherwise, the products spoil while the squabbling goes on. While they are arguing back and forth trying to negotiate, trying to deal, trying to do all kinds of things, the fresh produce deteriorates until, in some instances, it is not marketable.
The board of arbitration would give dealers an avenue of recourse. It would examine complaints about quality, packaging, storage, transportation and preservation of fruits and vegetables on the basis of standards and regulations made pursuant to the amendment of the CAPS Act. These regulations are currently being drawn up by a committee composed of both industry and Government members. Therefore, we can be sure that any new regulation will be practical enough for the industry to follow.
As you are probably aware, the United States is our major trading partner in fruits and vegetables. We are their largest customer. The United States operates an arbitration system to handle complaints where Canadian shippers arc involved. It is only reasonable that Canada should provide a similar service to settle disputes with our biggest trading partner.
Three other amendments to the CAPS Act concern the licensing and bonding of dealers in fresh fruits and vegetables.
December 16, 1982

Bill C-98 would amend the Act to provide for the licensing of such dealers and, secondly, to establish regulations setting out the terms and conditions surrounding a dealer's licence.
The third amendment to the Bill, approved last week by the Standing Committee on Agriculture, would require that all individuals and firms requiring licences would have to post a bond to cover any order or decision that might be made against them by the board. This amendment, I want to point out, was approved just last week by the Standing Committee after discussion with officials of the Fruit Wholesaler's Association and the Horticultural Council. An amount of $100,000 for the bond has been suggested, but the sum is still being discussed.
Members of the Canadian fruit and vegetable industry import hundreds of millions of dollars worth of perishable produce from all over the world each year. Thanks to them, Canadians can eat fresh spinach, bananas and melons and many other products all year round.

It is only reasonable that we should try to reduce some of the element or risk through the provision of a good arbitration service so as to make it fair and operate in a very smooth fashion.
We agree fully and, in a display of co-operation and awareness of a situation which has needed to be corrected since 1974, we have undertaken to pass as quickly as the Government of Canada will permit Bill C-98, the amendment to the CAPS Act.
The purpose of the amendment is to give the board of arbitration established under the CAPS Act binding powers when ruling over disputes regarding the condition of a product shipped and received, a dispute between shipper and receiver of fresh fruits and vegetables in national and international trade.
The House and the nation should take note that when legitimate, worthy legislation is advanced by this Government, the Opposition responds in a thoroughly constructive and helpful manner. On the other hand, when the Government puts forward legislation unworthy of support, which goes against the grain of our Canadian experience and tradition, the

Opposition will again respond in an equally thorough, constructive and helpful manner. In this instance we will accept our responsibility to resist, and explain to the electorate the reason for that resistance.
This is why the closure motion on the Canagrex Bill, C-85, brought the response which was demonstrated today. We resent the closing off of debate, limiting the ability of those in opposition to the measure to communicate to the general public the implications of that Bill.
The amendment to the Canadian Agricultural Products Standards Act is long overdue. The original Act, passed in 1934, was called the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act. My involvement in agriculture goes back quite a way. I remember when that Act was brought in. My father was active in the fruit industry, both the politics and the practical end of fruit growing in those days. The Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act brought a degree of stability and value to the industry that had previously been missing.
1 grew up on a fruit farm in the Okanagan Valley. As I said, my father was active in the practical side of fruit growing and the politics of the fruit industry. In those days it was a struggle to market a product that we grew in British Columbia and had to ship many miles across the country and to Europe. Presently we ship across the Pacific. The type of regulation brought to bear by the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act was an absolute imperative to the progress of that industry in British Columbia.
I can remember as a boy when my father was involved in protests, when fruit was shipped out of the Okanagan on consignment with no way of knowing what the ultimate return would be. There was a battle cry in those days when trains were stopped by the farming community. The battle cry was, "A cent a pound or on the ground." One reason we have upgraded the industry is that we had an act which provided uniform standards for the commodity we grow so well in the Okanagan Valley. We have an industry there now that produces values in the area of $150 million annually, which is a boost not just to the local economy, but to the Canadian economy as well. That is my background. I am a man of the soil.

subtopic: EMERGENCY MEASURES-GOVERNMENT PLANS. (B) ROLE OF PROVINCES
EMERGENCY MEASURES-GOVERNMENT PLANS. (B) ROLE OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the past 15 months or so I have been asking various Government Ministers questions dealing with the emergency planning orders that were passed by order in council in May of 1981. At first the Government denied the existence of these orders. Once they were found to be there, it said, "We have to do our planning". I think all Canadians will recognize that when it comes to emergencies, an orderly Government will plan for them.
Things became a little more ominous when the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) met with some of the provincial Ministers in June 1981 and told them in a speech that if the emergency plans were not completed, the Government might have to act extra-legally. That in itself was ominous enough but in the intervening 15 months we have found out, more and more, what the Government meant by acting extralegally.
Setting aside the order itself, which empowers a Solicitor General in wartime to depopulate prisons in order to make room for political hostages or political prisoners, and setting aside the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has total control of all the information agencies in the country-setting all those things aside-the President of the Privy Council only talked about acting extra-legally when it came to an emergency. We now find that the Government has made plans to act extra-legally if need be in order to design the order itself.
I want to bring to the attention of Members of the House the fact that about a month or six weeks ago a package came to my office. It contained the confidential memo sent to the President of the Privy Council from Mr. Snarr, the gentleman he appointed to head up the emergency planning agency. That memo outlined some pitfalls in federal-provincial relations that came to Mr. Snarr's attention through letters he received from some of the provincial Governments. Strategy was outlined as to how they might circumvent some of the problems. For the record I want to read some of the concerns which some of the Provinces have voiced.
First, I have a letter dated August 19 which came from an official of the Province of Alberta. It reads, in part:
The most obvious examples of such emergencies are situations of war or situations of transition from war to peace. Alberta is seriously concerned however, that the proposed federal legislation will not necessarily be confined to emergencies of an overriding national concern but that it also contemplates federal authority in what may be very localized situations.
On page 2, the letter continues:
It is my recommendation that a clear statement be made as to the temporary nature of the proposed legislation and that the legislation be confined to dealing explicitly with national emergencies that threaten the safety of Canada as a whole. Moreover, because of the extraordinary and constitutional features of the contemplated legislation, I would propose that full and complete consultation be undertaken with the provinces before the legislation is introduced to Parliament.
I have a copy of a letter sent to the President of the Privy Council, from a Minister in the former NDP Government of Saskatchewan. In part, this letter reads:
It has come to my attention that certain agencies and departments of this and other provincial Governments have been directly approached by federal officials with the intention of initiating joint planning processes. In the case of Saskatchewan and other provinces, this was done without the knowledge or consent of the Minister or officials responsible for emergency response and planning.
The letter continues:
Indeed, the discussion paper which we agreed to (No. 1-Joint Emergency Planning) specified that each province would "determine the form and nature of the planning mechanism best suited to its individual requirements", and that the "Provincial Emergency Measures Directors and the Regional Directors of Emergency Planning Canada will jointly facilitate and co-ordinate the planning of the joint emergency response arrangements."
This proposed arrangement seems to have been overlooked in the recent actions of numerous federal departments.
As you are aware, 1 and other provincial ministers attending the June 5th meeting in Ottawa had serious reservations about the form and possible scope of Planning Order PC 1305.
And the letter continues:
It now appears that federal emergency officials have seen no need to consult with their provincial counterparts, or to act in manner consistent with the agreement of Ministers, in initiating joint emergency planning processes. Numerous contacts have been made in Saskatchewan by federal emergency officials, and by line department officials, in reference to joint planning exercises or activities under P. O. 1305. In none of these instances has the provincial emergency staff been contacted by federal staffs in accordance with our understandings.
Finally, I have a letter from a Minister in the Government of Ontario in which it is stated that that Government is concerned and suggests that:
-the effect of suspending rights and freedoms guaranteed by the Charter of Rights ought to be brought into effect only in the clearest case of an emergency.
Further on in this letter we find:
The examples under which a state of emergency could be declared, as outlined in your statement, are far too broad and vague for Ontario to consent to federal pre-emption of its constitutional authority in such circumstances. 1 realize, of course, that further discussions could make our joint and individual interests much clearer than unilateral statements of our intent.
Mr. Snarr writes on page 3, paragraph (b) of his memo to the President of the Privy council that he proposes that the strategy regarding relations with the provinces should proceed and that they should:
-continue within the federal Government, our planning for NEAs, but in dealing with the provinces we would "soft-pedal", peacetime activation and for the time being concentrate on wartime interfaces between NEAs and provincial government facilities-
In paragraphs (d) and (e) he says they would continue the Joint Emergency Planning Program and the funding as long as the Provinces would co-operate. If they would refuse to cooperate, however, they would withdraw that funding, take it
December 16, 1982

over by the Government departments themselves and initiate those programs under the federal aegis; all that in the name of federal-provincial co-operation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: EMERGENCY MEASURES-GOVERNMENT PLANS. (B) ROLE OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am not here tonight to deny the authenticity of this particular document, or to dwell on the questionable ethics of making free use of classified material in the House. What I propose to do is to remind Hon. Members why the Access to Information Act we recently passed specifically removes such forms of privileged, communications from its general thrust.
In the intense and sometimes difficult world of federal-provincial relations, Ministers frequently receive advice from their officials in memoranda, such as the one in question, in which various options were outlined. Ministers are, of course, free to make use of this advice or to disregard it as they see fit.
In the case at hand, we are dealing with a document that is now some 14 months old. Despite what the Hon. Member has intimated, the memo has not seen the collapse of federal-provincial understanding in emergency planning. On the contrary, a number of events have taken place since October of
1981.
First, a federal-provincial conference of officials in January,
1982,	began the drafting of a intergovernmental Memorandum of Understanding on Emergency Planning covering both general principles and specific tasks.
In October of 1982, the federal Government and the Province of New Brunswick signed the first such memorandum, and discussions are continuing toward this end with eight other Provinces and with the two Territories.
Third, senior federal officials have held bilateral consultations on emergency planning with both Territories and with the Provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario and New Brunswick.
Fourth, applications for cost-shared projects under the Joint Emergency Planning Program have been received from both Territories and nine Provinces.
There have been 31 joint projects approvals under this particular program since October of 1981, including at least one from each Territory and every Province except Alberta.
Federal and Territorial officials will meet again in Winnipeg in February of 1983 to continue this important work.
I believe that these demonstrate that whatever options may have been outlined in the document under discussion, the course which has actually been followed has been one of free and open co-operation with the Provinces.
The practical reason why tactical advice prepared for Ministers is privileged in our Act is that it is all too easily misunderstood and misinterpreted. I believe that the present case is a classic example and I have to question whether the Hon. Member in raising this matter at the present hour is helping or hindering progress toward a more constructive working relationship between the federal and provincial Governments in the area of emergency planning.
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: ENERGY-COST COMPENSATION REQUESTED FOR HOME OWNERS IN NOVA SCOTIA. (B) EQUALIZATION OF ENERGY COSTS
ENERGY-COST COMPENSATION REQUESTED FOR HOME OWNERS IN NOVA SCOTIA. (B) EQUALIZATION OF ENERGY COSTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 26, 1982, I addressed a question in the House of Commons to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) concerning the cost of energy in the Maritime Provinces, particularly in the Province of Nova Scotia.
My purpose in questioning the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on this point was to present to him the problem that exists in the Province of Nova Scotia, and particularly in the Province of Prince Edward Island with respect to the tremendous burden on the consumers of home heating oil and other forms of energy which are utilized to heat homes. I was attempting to make the case for federal Government assistance to people in the Maritime Provinces, particularly the Province of Nova Scotia; for special aid to assist the residents of Nova Scotia in bearing these tremendous costs which have increased dramatically over the past few years. I welcome the opportunity now to make the case for special federal assistance to residents of Nova Scotia with respect to energy costs. I can only hope-perhaps forlornly-that my colleague from Nova Scotia, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Dingwall) will carry that message back to the Minister in the hope that some action may be taken before this winter passes.
In October of 1980, when the Government introduced its National Energy Program, it was stated that the Government would involve itself in the construction of a pipeline extension so that natural gas would be available in the Maritimes, particularly in Nova Scotia, by 1983. The importance of that promise made in the National Energy Program was that that natural gas was to be made available to Nova Scotians and other residents of the Maritimes at the Toronto city price, which would have amounted to substantially less than the cost of heating a home in Nova Scotia with oil or electricity, the basic methods of home heating in that Province.
That premise was reaffirmed several times in this House of Commons. This very year, 1982, in the National Energy Program update issued by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources the promise was repeated. The Government again said that it had a commitment to the extension of reasonably priced natural gas service to the Maritimes. Therefore, the Government did not forget the promise it made in 1980, even though it did nothing to implement the gas pipeline extension; it repeated the promise in 1982.
What we are concerned with now is the implementation of that promise because the Government has not succeeded in extending the gas pipeline. It can only fulfil its promise by providing financial aid to make up for the harm incurred by Nova Scotians and other Maritimers because of the failure to extend the pipeline.
In specific terms, that harm amounts to this. Home heating oil in Halifax at the present time, by way of example, is $1.46

December 16, 1982
Adjournment Debate
a gallon. It is known that the price for natural gas available in places like Toronto is approximately 67 per cent of the price of petroleum products, particularly home heating oil. Consequently, if that kind of price regime applied to consumers of home heating oil in Nova Scotia, the effective price would be 99 cents a gallon; that is to say, equating natural gas to home heating oil in relation to price, we would find that Nova Scotians would be paying a price of 99 cents instead of the current price of $1.46 a gallon for oil.
This means, in general terms, and I hope Your Honour follows my point, that instead of paying $1,168 a year over the winter months to heat the average home in Nova Scotia, a Nova Scotian family would be paying something like $792 if they had available a price equivalent to the natural gas price. That would mean a savings per family of $376 per year. If one multiplies that by the number of homes in Nova Scotia, over 200,000, one is talking about $80 million.
The point is that because the Government did not fulfil its promise to extend the natural gas pipeline to the Maritimes, particularly Nova Scotia, this very winter Nova Scotians will be paying $80 million more to heat their homes, and that is a conservative estimate because it includes only those people using home heating oil.
Therefore, what I want the Government to do is to consider this situation, consider the promise it made to Nova Scotians, consider the fact that that promise has been broken, and remedy the situation by providing equivalent financial aid.
In these days of cutbacks in Government expenditures, one might ask, where will the Government get the funds to provide this assistance? The fact is that, through the Petroleum Compensation Program, which the Government introduced, allegedly to help Nova Scotians and people on the East Coast to cushion the effects of increases in the cost of oil and home heating oil, as Your Honour knows, the Government provides a compensation program. That compensation paid in respect of oil imported to the East Coast of Canada cost over $3 billion in the last two fiscal years. Of course the price of foreign oil and the price of Canadian oil have come closer together. The price difference has now narrowed. The Government will spend substantially less this year and in the following years than it has in the past two years. This expenditure of approximately $3 billion will be reduced to something in the order of $1.5 billion.
So, Mr. Speaker, the $1.5 billion that the Government is saving in the payments it has been making through the Petroleum Compensation Board in respect of imports of oil should now be available to assist consumers with this increase in cost they are incurring, to heat their homes and for other energy purposes.
That is my request to the Minister, and I hope his Parliamentary Secretary will convey the message to him. Since the Government is saving $1.5 billion and since it has broken its
promise to deliver natural gas to Nova Scotia, causing consumers there an expenditure of over $80 million a year, some of this money should be used to offset that expenditure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) has raised the particular question, what assistance is the federal Government giving or going to give to the consumers in the Province of Nova Scotia?
I suggest at the outset that the Hon. Member for Halifax West must be running scared to be raising issues of this nature. He knows very well the reasons the pipeline is not proceeding as quickly as we would like. He knows that the Premier of the Province of Nova Scotia has indicated, in agreement with the Government of Canada, that if there is a delay in construction of that pipeline, so be it, because they are now finding natural gas in commercial quantities off the coast of Nova Scotia. Hopefully it will be possible to bring this onstream in the construction of the pipeline, and I am surprised that a Consservative Member of Parliament from Nova Scotia would be in disagreement with the Conservative Government of that Province.
The Hon. Member referred very briefly to the Oil Import Compensation Program. I suggest to the Hon. Member that he ought to take note of the facts. It should be noted that from January 1, 1974 to December 1, 1982, the Oil Import Compensation Program made payments to Nova Scotia totalling over $2.6 billion, yet he has the audacity to ask us what the Government of Canada is doing for Nova Scotia!
1 suggest to the Hon. Member that, in addition to the Oil Import Compensation Program, we should look at the Cape Breton Development Corporation which is being subsidized by the Government of Canada. That Crown corporation and the coal miners who work for it are getting substantially less for the product, which they sell primarily to the Nova Scotia Government, thereby keeping heating costs down. So it is the coal miners in Cape Breton who are subsidizing, to a large extent with the assistance of the Government of Canada, the Nova Scotia Power Corporation.
I suggest, with all due respect, that the Hon. Member for Halifax West, who is running scared obviously because of the political boundary changes which may occur in that Province, ought to embrace his Tory Premier and look at the facts. What he ought to do is to say to the Premier of Nova Scotia that the coal miners of Cape Breton ought to receive a better price for their coal. That is what he ought to be saying. But The Hon. Member refuses to acknowledge those facts. I can only say that I will take his representations under advisement.

subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-BANFF LAND EXCHANGE-ROLE OF CHAMBER OF COMMERCE. (B) REASON FOR REQUESTING DELAY IN DEVELOPMENT PROJECT. (C) REQUEST THAT BULLDOZERS BE REMOVED
NATIONAL PARKS-BANFF LAND EXCHANGE-ROLE OF CHAMBER OF COMMERCE. (B) REASON FOR REQUESTING DELAY IN DEVELOPMENT PROJECT. (C) REQUEST THAT BULLDOZERS BE REMOVED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this part of the Late Show tonight depicts a tragedy. A beautiful park, developed with taxpayers' money over a period of ten years by
December 16, 1982

Parks Canada, with benches for people to rest, with bridges over the stream, with paths for quiet walks so that all could enjoy nature, the birds, the 100 year-old trees and the animals, was destroyed, desecrated by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) in charge of national parks. The Minister allowed men with chainsaws to cut down the trees, bulldozers to tear up the paths so his friend, the Hon. Judd Buchanan, could build an apartment building on the site.
The Minister, knowing he had done wrong, steadfastly refused to investigate. When the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) was asked to freeze the project until a full inquiry was held, the Minister shook his head violently when the Deputy Prime Minister looked at him before answering the question in the House of Commons. He then meekly replied that he could see no reason to investigate. The head of any responsible Government would at least have looked into the matter before condoning it.
What were the Minister's excuses? First, he alleged he had telegrams from the Chamber of Commerce supporting his decision. In fact, he received one telegram over the name of the Banff-Lake Louise Chamber of Commerce which was sent by one or two men without the knowledge of the membership of the Chamber of Commerce, and one telegram, with the knowledge of the Chamber of Commerce, rescinding the first telegram. The Minister calls that support!
Second, the Minister alleged he had the support of the Banff Community Society when in fact that society on at least two occasions told the Minister it supported affordable housing, but asked that any decision to build in the park be held back until at least there was full public disclosure. The Minister conveniently forgot to mention that.
Third, the Minister misled the House by stating that the area had been zoned for multi purposes back in 1970 and that the people knew about it. The fact is it was so zoned and Parks Canada started the development of the park, but the Minister well knows that the people were not told in 1970 that a 76-unit apartment building was going to replace the park. It was only in late 1982 when a leak was published in The Crag and Canyon that the people found out about the under-the-table deal. Yes, it is true that near the end of 1981 it was discovered what was afoot, but the Deputy Minister in a letter stated emphatically that Parks Canada and Treasury Board had not approved the project. This again is a Government misleading the people.
Fourth, the Minister did not refer the case to Treasury Board, alleging that departmental officials did not consider it necessary. The people of Canada have been led to believe that Treasury Board decides whether a project should or should not be approved, which is a check on departmental expenditures. The Minister's action in this regard is hypocrisy of the worst kind.
Adjournment Debate
Fifth, the Minister likewise deliberately avoided referring the matter to the Federal Environmental Assessment Review Office (FEARO). The Minister justifies his actions because affordable accommodation is needed in Banff. Everyone agrees that affordable accommodation is needed, but no one wants it in the only treed park in the townsite. No one wants it in the park. The Minister admitted in committee that he had no guarantees from the developers that the accommodation will be affordable. They said it will be as affordable as possible, but $600 and $800 per month is not affordable accommodation.
In summary, this matter was carried out without letting the people know what was going on. It was done under the table and a park was destroyed. It is a tragedy that will forever stand to the dishonour of a man who dares to continue to be the Minister of the Environment in charge of National Parks.
